Bill Gates offered his childhood friend Paul Allen $5 per share to buy him out of Microsoft. Allen refused and kept the stock that would eventually help make him worth an estimated $40B.

Months earlier, while Allen was undergoing cancer treatment, he had overheard Gates and Steve Ballmer discussing how to reduce his ownership in the company they had built together.

The 2 had known each other since school.

Allen was 15 when he met 13-year-old Gates. They spent their teenage years working with computers and eventually founded Microsoft in 1975.

But the ownership split had been a source of tension from the beginning.

Gates initially wanted 60% of the company.

Allen got 40%.

Later, Gates pushed for another adjustment.

64% for himself.

36% for Allen.

Allen agreed.

Microsoft kept growing. Its deal to supply software for IBM's personal computer put the business on a completely different trajectory.

Then, in 1982, Allen was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

He began radiation treatment and gradually reduced his involvement in the company.

One evening in December, he walked past Gates' office.

Gates was talking with Steve Ballmer.

According to Allen, they were discussing his reduced productivity and how they could dilute his Microsoft equity by issuing stock options to themselves and others.

Allen stopped outside the door and listened.

Then he walked in.

He confronted both men and left.

That evening, Ballmer came to his house to apologize.

Days later, Gates sent a handwritten apology.

6 pages long.

But Allen had decided to leave.

In February 1983, he resigned from Microsoft.

Gates offered to buy his shares for $5 each.

Allen wanted at least $10.

Gates wouldn't pay it.

So Allen kept his stock.

When Microsoft went public in 1986, Allen still owned roughly 25% of the company.

As Microsoft grew into one of the world's largest businesses, his shares made him one of the richest people alive.

At one point, his fortune was estimated at $40B.

The 2 friends eventually repaired their relationship.

But Allen never forgot the conversation he overheard during his cancer treatment.

Gates had offered him $5 a share to leave.

Allen left.

His shares stayed.

It’s a no brainer if general welfare is the consideration.

In March 2019, 61-year-old Cecile Eledge gave birth to a healthy baby girl in Nebraska.

The baby was her own granddaughter.

Her son and his husband needed a surrogate. When Cecile volunteered, they thought it was a joke.

She had already gone through menopause, but after extensive testing, doctors approved her to carry the baby.

Using IVF, they combined her son's sperm with an egg from his husband's sister and placed the embryo in Cecile's womb.

Nine months later, she delivered the baby with both fathers by her side. That made Cecile both her granddaughter's surrogate and her biological grandmother.
